I'm tracing through the USB device enumeration flow to identify where the issue originates. When a USB device is detected behind a Type-C port, `typec_partner_attach` gets invoked, which stores the device reference and then attempts to link it to any existing partner through `typec_partner_link_device`.

The critical problem emerges when `typec_partner_link_device` fails silently on `sysfs_create_link` errors — the device pointer remains stored in `port->usb2_dev` or `port->usb3_dev` even though the symlink was never created. Later, when `typec_unregister_partner` tries to clean up by calling `typec_partner_unlink_device`, it attempts to remove a symlink that doesn't exist, triggering a kernel warning in the `kernfs_remove_by_name_ns` function.

The race condition happens when a UCSI connector change fires during USB device enumeration or disconnection, creating a timing mismatch between when the device pointers are set and when the symlinks are actually created or removed.

The core issue is that `typec_partner_link_device` can fail silently without reporting an error, leaving the device pointer stored in `port->usbX_dev` even though no symlink was created. Later, when the partner unregisters, the code unconditionally tries to remove a symlink that never existed, triggering the kernfs warning.

The failure happens when `sysfs_create_link` returns -EEXIST because a "typec" link already exists on that device — which occurs when both usb2_dev and usb3_dev point to the same struct device, or when a second partner tries to link to the same USB device. In a typical dual-role scenario like a Dell dock, the USB 2.0 and 3.x devices are separate, so each gets its own link without conflict. But if a USB device re-enumerates at a different speed on the same connector, the second partner attachment tries to create a duplicate link on the same device object.

The real issue is that the code tracks link state implicitly through non-NULL pointers in port->usb2_dev and usb3_dev, but `typec_partner_link_device()` silently ignores `sysfs_create_link()` failures, and `typec_register_partner()` only creates links at registration time — so stale pointers and failed link creations go undetected.

When `typec_unregister_partner()` tries to remove a link that was never successfully created, `sysfs_remove_link()` returns -ENOENT and triggers the warning. There's also a race condition where `typec_partner_deattach()` unlinks under the partner_link_lock while `typec_unregister_partner()` tries to unlink the same link, and if USB disconnect happens at the wrong moment, both paths execute. `typec_get_partner()` searches for the partner device using the device tree, so even if the partner is mid-unregistration, it might still be found. The upstream fix I should reference is commit 8dc82a37449e which adds the partner_link_lock — and that lock is already present in this codebase, so the core synchronization is there.

There's a known issue on Dell/Intel UCSI systems about "kernfs: can not remove 'typec'" warnings, likely related to symlink removal timing. I recall a patch addressing this by tracking whether the symlink was actually created before attempting removal, but I can't confirm the exact upstream commit hash without verification.
